params.title: Satellite
params.subtitle: How Iridium, COSPAS-SARSAT, Inmarsat and GPS work: their orbits, frequencies, services and antennas.

scenes.narration: Welcome to Satellite. Far out at sea, beyond the reach of radio stations on shore, a ship relies on satellites to make phone calls, send messages, raise the alarm in a disaster, and know exactly where it is. In this lesson we'll meet the 4 satellite systems that do those jobs: Iridium, COSPAS-SARSAT, Inmarsat, and GPS, the Global Positioning System. We'll start from what a satellite and an orbit are, so you don't need any background. By the end, you'll be able to compare the 4 systems by how high they orbit, which frequencies they use, what services they offer and what antennas they need, which is exactly what the exam asks.

params.title: Why put a radio in space?

blocks.label: Satellite
blocks.note: A radio relay high above the Earth

onScreen: Satellite: a radio relay above the Earth
Direct path blocked by the Earth's curve
scenes.narration: Let's start with the problem satellites solve. Picture a ship far out at sea. The radio signals in this lesson travel in straight lines, much like light, so they can't follow the curve of the Earth past the horizon. The fix is a satellite: a radio relay placed high above the Earth, where it can see huge areas at once. The ship sends its signal up to the satellite, and the satellite passes it back down to a station on shore. The ship could never reach that station directly, because the curve of the Earth is in the way, the same curve that hides a distant ship below the horizon.

params.title: Low orbits and high orbits
rows: 1 day: it seems to hang still

onScreen: Low Earth orbit: a few hundred miles, about 100 minutes
Geostationary orbit: far higher, 1 day, seems to hang still
scenes.narration: But how does a satellite stay up there? It's in orbit, the path it follows around the Earth. It's actually falling the whole time, but moving sideways so fast that it keeps missing the ground. Gravity pulls hardest close to the Earth, so the lower the satellite, the faster it must go. In low Earth orbit, a few hundred miles up, it races around about once every 100 minutes. Higher up, a satellite moves slower along a longer path. At one special height above the equator, a trip takes 1 day, as long as the Earth takes to turn once. So it seems to hang still in the sky. That's a geostationary orbit: stationary over one spot on the Earth.

params.title: Iridium: low Earth orbit at 485 miles

scenes.narration: With those 2 kinds of orbit in mind, meet the first system. Iridium is a satellite telephone network: its phones talk straight to the satellites overhead. Iridium satellites orbit at an altitude, or height, of 485 miles, in low Earth orbit. Why so low? A nearby satellite can hear a small handheld phone clearly. The price is that each satellite sees only a small patch of the Earth and crosses the sky in minutes. So Iridium needs many satellites, and a call is handed from one to the next as they pass. The exam's wrong choices are all much higher. Iridium is the low one: 485 miles, far below the geostationary Inmarsat satellites at 22,177 miles, which we'll visit later.

params.title: What is a frequency?
labels: 1 cycle: one complete wave, up and back down
Frequency: cycles per second, in hertz
1 megahertz (MHz): a million cycles per second
Band: a range of frequencies set aside for one use

onScreen: Frequency: cycles per second, in hertz
1 megahertz: a million cycles per second
scenes.narration: Altitude is the first way to tell the systems apart. The second is frequency, so here's what a frequency is. A radio signal is an invisible wave of energy that swings up and down, over and over. One complete swing, up and back down, is called a cycle. The number of cycles each second is the frequency, measured in hertz: 1 hertz is 1 cycle per second. Radio waves swing extremely fast, so we count them in megahertz: 1 megahertz is a million cycles per second. A band is a range of frequencies set aside for one use, like one lane of a highway kept for one kind of traffic.

So which lane is Iridium's? Iridium uses the 1616 to 1626 megahertz band for telephone and messaging. The greyed bands are the exam's wrong choices: other bands, some lower and some higher, that Iridium doesn't use for its phones. Iridium's slice is 10 megahertz wide, and the width of a slice like that is called its bandwidth. The phone and the satellite share it, taking turns to talk. A handy way to remember the band: it starts with 16, twice. Pick 1616 to 1626 megahertz.

params.title: Analog or digital?
items: Analog: the signal copies the smooth shape of the sound
Digital: the voice is measured and sent as bits, 1s and 0s
kbps: kilobits per second, thousands of bits each second
Iridium: digital voice and data at 2.4 kbps, no analog voice

onScreen: kbps: thousands of bits per second
Iridium: digital voice and data at 2.4 kbps, no analog voice
scenes.narration: What does Iridium carry over that band? First, 2 words: analog and digital. In analog radio, the signal copies the smooth ups and downs of your voice. In digital radio, the voice is measured many times a second and turned into numbers, sent as bits: the 1s and 0s computers use. Bits can be checked and corrected, so digital speech stays clear even on a weak signal. Digital speed is counted in kilobits per second: thousands of bits each second. Iridium is all digital. It provides digital voice and data at 2.4 kilobits per second, with no analog voice at all. So any exam choice with analog voice, or a faster rate such as 9.6, is wrong.

params.title: Iridium spot beams
items: Footprint: the patch of Earth a satellite's antenna covers
Spot beam: a narrow beam aimed at one part of the footprint
Each Iridium satellite forms 48 spot beams
For the exam: 48 spot beams per satellite, 30-mile footprint
Really about 400 km, or 250 miles, across each beam

onScreen: Footprint: the area a satellite covers
Spot beam: a narrow beam within it
scenes.narration: One more Iridium exam question is about spot beams. A satellite's footprint is the patch of Earth its antenna covers. Rather than light that whole patch with one broad beam, like a floodlight, an Iridium satellite splits it into many narrow spot beams, like a cluster of flashlights. Each spot beam is stronger, and neighboring beams can carry different calls. Each Iridium satellite forms 48 spot beams. For the exam, the keyed answer is: there are 48 spot beams per satellite, with a footprint of 30 miles in diameter, meaning each beam's patch is 30 miles straight across. Choose it. The 48 is right, but each beam is really about 400 kilometers, or about 250 miles, across.

onScreen: Not 48 satellites in 4 planes: 66 in 6 planes
scenes.narration: Why are the other Iridium choices wrong? They describe the constellation, the whole group of satellites. Each orbit lies in a flat ring around the Earth called an orbital plane, like a hoop. Inclination is how far that hoop tilts from the equator: 0 degrees runs along the equator, and 90 degrees passes over the poles. Iridium is not 48 satellites in 4 orbital planes. It uses 66 active satellites in 6 planes inclined 86.4 degrees, so close to 90 that they're called near-polar, and together they cover the whole Earth, poles included. 55 degrees belongs to GPS, which we'll meet later. And the orbital period, the time for one trip around, is about 100 minutes, not 85.

callouts.label: Many float free and switch on if the ship sinks
Sends a distress call on 406 MHz
Strobe light helps rescuers spot it

scenes.narration: Iridium carries everyday calls. The other system that relies on low-orbit satellites has one life-saving job. Its name, COSPAS-SARSAT, joins a Russian name with an English one, SARSAT: search and rescue satellite-aided tracking. It listens for EPIRBs, emergency position-indicating radio beacons. An EPIRB is a small, tough transmitter carried on a ship. Many are mounted so they float free and switch on by themselves if the ship sinks. The beacon then sends a distress call on 406 megahertz, and a flashing strobe light helps rescuers spot it once they're close.

So what does the satellite do? The main function of COSPAS-SARSAT is to monitor 406 megahertz for distress calls from EPIRBs, and relay them to ground stations called local user terminals. The local user terminal works out where the beacon is and passes the alert to a rescue coordination center, which organizes the search. The exam's traps offer other frequencies, such as 121.5 megahertz, an older beacon frequency the satellites no longer listen for. The satellites listen on 406.

params.title: The Doppler shift
labels: Approaching: waves bunch up and are heard a little higher
Moving away: waves stretch out and are heard a little lower
At the closest point: no shift at all

onScreen: Moving away: heard a little lower
scenes.narration: How does the local user terminal know where the beacon is? The name says position-indicating, but not every EPIRB reports its position: only beacons with built-in GPS send their own coordinates. For the rest, it uses the Doppler shift, which you've heard on the street. An ambulance siren sounds higher coming toward you and lower moving away, though the siren itself never changes. Its motion bunches the sound waves up in front, so they arrive more often, and stretches them out behind. Radio waves do the same. A low-orbit satellite racing toward the beacon hears its 406 megahertz signal a little high, and a little low as it moves away. When it's closest, there's no shift at all.

params.title: Finding the beacon by Doppler
items: Shift passes through zero: the satellite is at its closest
Sharp swing from high to low: it passed nearly overhead
Together these give the beacon's position
Exam: Doppler shift of 406 MHz at several points in the orbit

onScreen: Doppler shift of 406 MHz at several points in the orbit
scenes.narration: That changing frequency is the clue. The moment the shift passes through zero tells the local user terminal when the satellite was closest to the beacon. How quickly the shift swings from high to low tells how far the beacon is from the satellite's path: a sharp swing means the satellite passed almost overhead. Put those together, and the terminal can work out where the beacon is. So, for the exam: COSPAS-SARSAT determines the position of a ship in distress by measuring the Doppler shift of the 406 megahertz signal, taken at several different points in its orbit.

params.title: Finding the beacon: the traps
rows: Doppler shift at several points in the orbit
The EPIRB always transmits its position
False: only beacons with built-in GPS

onScreen: True: Doppler shift at several points in the orbit
False: the EPIRB always sends its position
scenes.narration: The keyed answer is the Doppler one, and it shows why the system uses low orbits: a satellite that seemed to hang still would show no shift at all. Now the traps. The EPIRB always transmits its position? No: as we saw, only beacons with built-in GPS send their own coordinates, and the Doppler method works without them. It takes 2 different satellites? No: 1 satellite, measuring the shift at several points along its own pass, is enough. The takeaway for low orbits: close and fast, so small phones can reach them and Doppler can find a beacon.

onScreen: Inmarsat: 22,177 miles, geostationary above the equator
scenes.narration: Now we leave the low orbits and climb to the highest one in this lesson. Inmarsat, named for the International Maritime Satellite Organization that founded it, carries ships' phone calls, messages, data and distress alerts. Its satellites orbit at an altitude of 22,177 miles, in geostationary orbit above the equator. As you saw earlier, that means each trip around takes 1 day, so each satellite hangs over the same spot. A ship's antenna can stay pointed at it, and just a few satellites can cover most of the oceans. The exam's other altitudes are just wrong numbers, and one of them is even higher, so don't simply pick the biggest. Remember 22,177 miles, far above Iridium's 485.

params.title: Placing a geostationary satellite
items: Each satellite stays over one spot on the equator
So its longitude alone says where it is
Longitude: degrees east or west of Greenwich, England, at 0°
Inmarsat: 4 satellites, one for each ocean region

onScreen: Fixed over one spot on the equator
Its longitude says where it is
Longitude: degrees east or west of Greenwich
scenes.narration: Because a geostationary satellite never leaves its spot over the equator, you can say where it is with a single number: its longitude. Longitude measures how far east or west a place is, in degrees around the Earth, counted from 0 degrees, the line that runs from pole to pole through Greenwich, England. The classic Inmarsat system uses 4 satellites, one for each ocean region, the stretch of ocean it looks down on, and each region is named for that ocean. Let's place all 4.

Here is the Inmarsat satellite system, region by region, measured from Greenwich. AOR-E, the Atlantic Ocean Region East, is at 15.5 degrees west: of the 2 Atlantic satellites, East is the one nearer Greenwich. AOR-W, the Atlantic Ocean Region West, is at 54 degrees west, farther out toward the Americas. POR, the Pacific Ocean Region, is at 178 degrees east, almost halfway around the world. And IOR, the Indian Ocean Region, is at 64.5 degrees east. So both Atlantic satellites are west of Greenwich, and the Pacific and Indian ones are east. The trap answers invent regions such as POR-E or IOR-W, or shift the degrees, so learn these 4 exactly.

onScreen: Equator, 0°: satellites high in the sky
scenes.narration: How far can these 4 satellites reach? For that you need latitude: how far north or south of the equator a place is, from 0 degrees at the equator to 90 degrees at the poles. Since the satellites sit over the equator, a ship near the equator sees them high in the sky. Sail toward a pole, and the satellite sinks lower and lower toward the horizon, until the curve of the Earth hides it. Above about 70 degrees latitude, a ship can't use Inmarsat at all.

params.title: Inmarsat coverage: true or false?
rows: Covers nearly all the world's navigable waters
In polar orbit, for true global coverage
False: they sit over the equator
Equatorial orbit, for true global coverage
Equatorial waters can use only 1 satellite

onScreen: False: only 1 satellite near the equator
scenes.narration: So the true statement is: Inmarsat geostationary satellites provide coverage to vessels in nearly all of the world's navigable waters. Navigable waters are the seas ships actually sail, and few ships go above 70 degrees latitude. Now the traps. The satellites are not in polar orbit; they sit over the equator. Their orbit is equatorial, but that doesn't give true global coverage, because the polar regions above about 70 degrees are missed. And the claim that ships in equatorial waters can use only 1 satellite is also false: neighboring coverage areas overlap, and the overlaps are widest near the equator, right under the satellites. The takeaway: high, fixed, and nearly everywhere, but not at the poles.

blocks.label: Ship earth station
blocks.note: Sends a routine or distress message

blocks.label: Land earth station
blocks.note: Stores the message, then forwards it

blocks.label: Recipient
blocks.note: Gets it later: not real time

onScreen: Ship earth station sends a routine or distress message
Land earth station stores, then forwards
Recipient gets it later: not real time
scenes.narration: That's where Inmarsat reaches. Now, what can a ship do with it? Inmarsat offers several services, most named with a letter. Inmarsat-C is the simplest: a store-and-forward system that provides routine and distress communications, meaning everyday messages as well as distress alerts. Here's how store-and-forward works. The ship types a text message, and its ship earth station, the ship's satellite terminal, sends it up to the satellite. The satellite passes it down to a land earth station, a large ground station linked to the phone and data networks on land. The land earth station stores the whole message, then forwards it to the recipient, like posting a letter rather than making a phone call.

params.title: Inmarsat-C: true or false?
rows: False: messages wait at the land station
Slow speed telex and voice service

scenes.narration: So on the exam, the best description of Inmarsat-C is the store-and-forward one, for routine and distress communications. Each trap gets one detail wrong. It is not a real-time telex system. Telex is an older way of sending typed text between machines, where the words reach the other end as they're typed. Inmarsat-C messages wait at the land earth station first. It doesn't provide slow speed telex and voice either, because Inmarsat-C carries no voice at all. And it doesn't provide worldwide coverage: like all Inmarsat, it misses the polar regions.

params.title: Inmarsat-B: real-time voice, fax and data
items: Voice at 16 kbps
Fax at 14.4 kbps: a copy of a printed page
High-speed data at 64/54 kbps
All in real time, not store-and-forward

scenes.narration: Inmarsat-B is the opposite: a live connection, like a phone call. Its services start with voice at 16 kilobits per second. Next is fax, short for facsimile: a copy of a printed page, sent at 14.4 kilobits per second. Then comes high-speed data, which the exam writes as 64 slash 54 kilobits per second. All of it is delivered in real time, rather than store-and-forward. Notice how much faster these rates are than Iridium's 2.4. The store-and-forward choice is the trap here, because store-and-forward belongs to Inmarsat-C.

onScreen: Decoder turns bits back into speech
scenes.narration: How does a voice travel as bits? Like Iridium, Inmarsat-B is digital, so for voice communications via an Inmarsat-B terminal, CODECs are used to digitize the voice signal: turn it into bits. CODEC is short for coder-decoder. The coder measures your voice and turns it into a stream of bits. They cross the satellite link at 16 kilobits per second. At the far end, the decoder turns the bits back into sound. The traps: noise-blanking, selected by the operator, is a receiver feature for cutting out bursts of static. Compressing the voice to fit the bandwidth, or expanding it at the receiving end, may sound like CODEC work, but the exam keys the plain answer: digitizing.

params.title: Two kinds of antenna
rows: All directions, like a bare bulb
A narrow beam, like a flashlight
Works any way the ship points

onScreen: Omnidirectional: all directions, low gain, no aiming
Directional must be aimed and stabilized
scenes.narration: So far we've seen what Inmarsat-B and Inmarsat-C carry, and that decides what antenna each needs. There are 2 kinds. An omnidirectional antenna sends and receives about equally in all directions, like a bare light bulb. A directional antenna, such as a dish, focuses its energy into a narrow beam, like a flashlight. That focusing is called gain: it makes the signal much stronger, but only where the antenna points. On a rolling, turning ship, motors must keep a dish pointed at the satellite, which is called stabilization. Why does this matter? More bits each second need a stronger signal to arrive without errors. So faster data needs a stronger signal, and a stronger signal needs gain.

callouts.label: SES: ship earth station, the ship's satellite terminal
Works on any heading as the ship rolls and turns
Not a stabilized dish, a cardioid pattern or a narrow beam up

onScreen: Not a dish, a cardioid or a narrow beam
scenes.narration: Start with Inmarsat-C. It sends short text messages at a slow rate, so it doesn't need a strong, focused signal. The Inmarsat-C SES, or ship earth station, antenna is omnidirectional, so it needs no aiming or stabilization. It's a small unit that works on any heading, meaning whichever way the ship points, however it rolls and turns. On the exam, the traps all describe beams: a highly directional dish needing stabilization, a heart-shaped pattern off the front, which the exam calls cardioid, or a narrow beam straight up. None of them fits Inmarsat-C. The answer is omnidirectional.

params.title: Inmarsat-B versus Inmarsat-C antennas
rows: High gain for voice and fast data
Stabilized dish aimed at the satellite

onScreen: B needs high gain; C needs little
B is aimed and stabilized; C needs no aiming
scenes.narration: Put the 2 side by side. Inmarsat-C antennas are small and omnidirectional, while Inmarsat-B antennas are larger and directional. The reason is the data rate. Inmarsat-B's real-time voice and fast data need high gain. A bigger dish collects more of the signal, the way a wider bucket catches more rain, so it gives more gain, as long as it's aimed at the satellite and kept stabilized. Inmarsat-C's slow text gets by with little gain. The traps swap the details: an omnidirectional Inmarsat-B, an Inmarsat-C with a parabolic antenna, meaning a dish, or an Inmarsat-B dish described as smaller or lower gain. In short: C is small and omnidirectional; B is larger and directional.

callouts.label: The dish needs a clear line of sight to the satellite
A mast blocking the signal on a certain course
A satellite on a low elevation, below the horizon
Travel beyond the effective radius of the satellite
Any one makes it impossible: the answer is all of these

onScreen: Needs a clear line of sight
Mast blocking on a certain course
scenes.narration: That narrow beam has a weakness: the Inmarsat-B dish needs a clear line of sight to the satellite: an unblocked straight path. 3 conditions can make Inmarsat-B communications impossible. First, an obstruction, such as a mast, blocking the signal between the satellite and the SES antenna when the vessel steers a certain course. Second, a satellite on a low elevation, meaning low in the sky, below the horizon. Third, travel beyond the effective radius of the satellite, out of its coverage area. Any one of them is enough, so on the exam, the answer is all of these.

params.title: Inmarsat-M
items: Voice at 6.2 kbps
Data at 2.4 kbps
Fax at 2.4 kbps
Plus e-mail
A smaller antenna than Inmarsat-B

scenes.narration: That covers Inmarsat-B and Inmarsat-C, the 2 ends of the family. In between sits Inmarsat-M, a compact digital voice service. Inmarsat-M provides voice at 6.2 kilobits per second, lower than Inmarsat-B's 16, because it uses a low-rate CODEC that packs speech into fewer bits. It also provides data at 2.4 kilobits per second, fax at 2.4 kilobits per second, and e-mail. All of that works through a smaller antenna than Inmarsat-B needs. Watch for trap rates such as 4.8 and 9.6. Look for 6.2 for voice and 2.4 for data and fax.

params.title: Inmarsat mini-M
items: A satellite system utilizing spot beams
Spot beams focus the satellite's power on smaller areas
A stronger signal means a small, light antenna is enough
Provides for small craft communications

scenes.narration: Remember Iridium's spot beams? They're back. The Inmarsat mini-M system is a satellite system utilizing spot beams to provide for small craft communications. Instead of spreading its power over a whole ocean region, the satellite concentrates it into narrower spot beams aimed at chosen areas. With a stronger signal arriving, a small, light antenna is enough, which suits yachts and other small craft. The traps call mini-M a sonar or a depth finder, which are underwater sound devices, or a global satellite system, which it isn't, because its spot beams cover only chosen areas. It's the spot beam system for small craft.

params.title: High-speed data at 64/54 kbps
items: Fast data needs a strong signal: high gain
High gain needs a directional antenna
Inmarsat-B, M4 and Fleet have one
Inmarsat-C and mini-M don't: small antennas, slow data

onScreen: High gain needs a directional antenna
scenes.narration: Now that you've met the whole family, one last Inmarsat question brings back the gain idea. Which systems offer high-speed data at 64 slash 54 kilobits per second? Fast data needs a strong signal, a strong signal needs high gain, and high gain needs a directional antenna. Inmarsat-B, M4 and Fleet have one, so they're the answer. M4 and Fleet are later Inmarsat services built around that same kind of aimed antenna. The traps are Inmarsat-C alone, B and C together, and mini-M. Inmarsat-C and mini-M use small antennas that limit them to slow data, so any choice that includes them is wrong.

params.title: The Inmarsat services side by side
rows: Voice 6.2, data and fax 2.4 kbps, e-mail
Small craft calls via spot beams

onScreen: Inmarsat-M: voice 6.2, data and fax 2.4 kbps
Mini-M: spot beams for small craft
scenes.narration: Here's the Inmarsat family in one view. Inmarsat-B: real-time voice at 16, fax at 14.4 and data at 64 slash 54 kilobits per second, through a larger directional dish. Inmarsat-C: routine and distress text, store-and-forward, no voice, through a small omnidirectional antenna. Inmarsat-M: voice at 6.2, data and fax at 2.4, plus e-mail. And mini-M: spot beams serving small craft. The rule of thumb: the faster the service, the bigger and more directional the antenna.

blocks.label: GPS satellite
blocks.note: Broadcasts its exact time and position

blocks.label: Ship's GPS receiver
blocks.note: Measures how long the signal took

blocks.label: Distance to that satellite
blocks.note: Travel time at the speed of light

onScreen: GPS satellite broadcasts its time and position
scenes.narration: That completes Inmarsat. Our last system works differently. Iridium, COSPAS-SARSAT and Inmarsat all carry messages. GPS, the Global Positioning System, does something else: it tells you where you are, and what time it is. Each GPS satellite carries a very precise clock and keeps broadcasting its exact time and position. A GPS receiver on the ship picks up that signal and checks how long it took to arrive. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, so the travel time tells the distance to that satellite. Distances to several satellites, as we'll see, pin down the ship's position.

onScreen: GPS: 12,554 miles, about once every 12 hours
scenes.narration: Where are the GPS satellites? GPS satellites orbit at an altitude of 12,554 miles, circling the Earth about once every 12 hours, which is twice a day. That's called a medium Earth orbit, and it completes our picture. Iridium is far below, in low Earth orbit at 485 miles. Inmarsat is far above, in geostationary orbit at 22,177 miles. So from low to high, it's Iridium, then GPS, then Inmarsat. Remember that order, and the exam's altitude questions get much easier.

params.title: 24 GPS satellites
items: 24 GPS satellites normally in operation
6 orbital planes × 4 satellites each = 24
Extra satellites kept in orbit as spares
At least 4 in view from anywhere on Earth

scenes.narration: How many GPS satellites are there? 24 GPS satellites are normally in operation, 4 in each orbital plane. An orbital plane, you'll recall, is the hoop an orbit lies in. GPS uses 6 of them, and 6 planes times 4 satellites is 24. Extra satellites are kept in orbit as spares, in case one fails. The 24 are spread out so that at least 4 are in view from anywhere on Earth, which, as you'll see, is exactly what a receiver needs. The exam's wrong counts are 8, 18 and 36. The answer is 24.

params.title: GPS orbits: true or false?
rows: 4 planes spaced 90° in a polar orbit

scenes.narration: Now the shape of those orbits. GPS satellites are in 6 orbital planes, equally spaced and inclined about 55 degrees to the equator. Picture 6 tilted hoops spread evenly around the Earth. Iridium's 86.4 degrees is nearly polar; GPS's 55 is well short of that, so GPS orbits are not polar. Nor are they geosynchronous. Geosynchronous means an orbit that takes 1 day; geostationary, like Inmarsat, is the kind that sits over the equator. GPS takes 12 hours. So the traps fail: not 4 polar planes spaced 90 degrees, not geosynchronous over the equator, and not 8 planes at about 1,000 miles.

Next, the timing signals themselves: they go out on 2 frequencies. The GPS transmitted frequencies are 1227.6 megahertz and 1575.4 megahertz. Don't mix them up with the other satellite frequencies in this lesson. Just above GPS is Iridium's 1616 to 1626 megahertz band for telephone and messaging, and far below is 406 megahertz, where COSPAS-SARSAT listens for EPIRBs. On the exam, watch the digits: one trap pairs 946.2 with 1226.6, which looks almost like 1227.6. The right pair is 1227.6 and 1575.4.

params.title: From distances to a position
items: 1 distance: somewhere on a sphere around that satellite
2 distances: on the circle where the 2 spheres cross
3 distances: 2 points, and only 1 is near the Earth
But only if the receiver's clock is perfect

scenes.narration: So how does the receiver turn travel times into a position? Each travel time gives a distance. Knowing you're a certain distance from one satellite puts you somewhere on a giant imaginary ball, a sphere, centered on it. A second distance narrows that down to the circle where the 2 spheres cross. A third leaves just 2 possible points, and only 1 of them is anywhere near the Earth. So in principle, 3 satellites would be enough. But there's a catch. Radio covers about a foot in a billionth of a second, so a tiny clock error becomes a big distance error. The satellites carry costly atomic clocks, but a receiver has an ordinary one, and it's never perfect.

onScreen: 4 satellites for complete position and time
scenes.narration: The way around it: the receiver treats its own clock error as one more thing to solve for. Count the unknowns: latitude, longitude, altitude, and the receiver's clock error. That's 4 unknowns. Like a puzzle where each clue settles one thing, solving for 4 unknowns takes 4 measurements, one from each of 4 satellites. So 4 satellites must be received to provide complete position and time. With only 3, a receiver can give a position only by assuming its altitude. That's why 1, 2 and 3 are wrong on the exam. The answer is 4.

params.title: Why GPS needs a helper
items: GPS positions still carry small errors
One cause: signals slowed in the upper atmosphere
A station at a known spot can measure the error
Nearby receivers have nearly the same error

onScreen: Signals slowed in the upper atmosphere
A known spot can measure the error
scenes.narration: Even with 4 satellites, a GPS position isn't perfect. Small errors creep in, for example as the signals slow slightly passing through the upper atmosphere. Here's the clever part. Imagine a station that already knows exactly where it stands, because its spot has been carefully surveyed, that is, measured exactly. It can compare that true position with what GPS tells it, and the difference is the error. A ship nearby is receiving the same satellites through nearly the same sky, so it has nearly the same error.

blocks.label: Reference station
blocks.note: Precisely surveyed: measures the GPS error

onScreen: Reference station at a precisely surveyed location measures the error
Ship's GPS receiver applies the corrections
Correction factors from the station to the ship
scenes.narration: That idea is DGPS, Differential GPS. It is a system to provide additional correction factors to improve position accuracy. A reference station at a precisely surveyed location measures the error in the GPS signals it receives and broadcasts correction factors. A ship's receiver applies them, and its position becomes more accurate. Note that D stands for differential, not digital. The corrections come from the reference station, not from the GPS satellites themselves, and DGPS isn't just altitude corrections for aircraft. It's correction factors for better position accuracy.

onScreen: GPS: 24 satellites, 4 for a fix; DGPS corrections
scenes.narration: Let's wrap up with the 5 things to carry into the exam. From low to high: Iridium at 485 miles, GPS at 12,554, Inmarsat at 22,177. Iridium talks on 1616 to 1626 megahertz, and GPS transmits on 1227.6 and 1575.4. COSPAS-SARSAT listens for EPIRBs on 406 megahertz and finds them by the Doppler shift. Inmarsat-C uses a small omnidirectional antenna and stores and forwards text, while Inmarsat-B needs a larger directional dish for real-time voice, fax and fast data. Finally, GPS has 24 satellites in 6 planes inclined 55 degrees, you need 4 of them for complete position and time, and DGPS sharpens the fix with correction factors from a surveyed reference station. Well done.
